L983@P21: B.1 UNDERSTANDING THE TRADE-OFFS BETWEEN THE JOINT AND MARGINAL MODELS
L984@P21: Figure 5: Quantitative comparison of the marginal and joint prediction models. Left: The
L985@P21: marginal minADE broken down as a function of number of predicted agents. When there are more
L986@P21: agents, producing internally consistent predictions is more challenging, and hence the joint model
L987@P21: performs slightly worse. Right: Overlap rate between pairs of agent predictions. The joint model
L988@P21: produces internally consistent predictions with lower inter-prediction overlap rates.
L989@P21: While the joint mp-only model performs better on the interactive prediction task than the marginal
L990@P21: model when evaluated with joint metrics, it performs worse on the motion prediction task when
L991@P21: evaluated with marginal metrics (see Table 11 "ours (joint)"). This is because the joint model is
L992@P21: trained to produce predictions that are internally consistent between agents, while the marginal model
L993@P21: does not, which is a strictly harder task. In this section, we examine this quality difference and the
L994@P21: internal consistency of the predictions from both models.
L995@P21: In the WOMD dataset, each example has a different number of agents to be predicted. By slicing
L996@P21: the marginal minADE results based on the number of agents to be predicted (Figure 5, left), we find
L997@P21: that the joint model performs worse as there are more predicted agents, while the marginal model
L998@P21: performs the same. This is expected: when there are more agents, the joint model has a more difficult
L999@P21: task since it needs to produce internally consistent predictions. One may expect a joint model to need
L1000@P21: an exponential number of trajectory combinations to perform competitively with the marginal model,
L1001@P21: but we are encouraged to find that this is not actually the case. We believe this is due to the fact that
L1002@P21: when many agents are interacting, the number of realistic scenarios is actually heavily constrained by
L1003@P21: interactions - most combinations of marginal predictions don’t actually make sense together.
L1004@P21: However, when more agents are to be predicted, the possibility of interactions are higher and we
L1005@P21: would expect that the joint model is able to capture these interactions through internally consistent
L1006@P21: predictions. We measure the models’ internal consistency by selecting the best trajectory and
L1007@P21: measuring the inter-prediction overlap rate (details below). We find that the joint model has a
L1008@P21: consistently lower inter-prediction overlap rate, showing that it is able to capture the interactions
L1009@P21: between agents. The ability to model interactions enables the model to be suitable for conditional
L1010@P21: motion prediction, and goal conditioned prediction tasks, which we discuss in Section 4.4.
L1011@P21: Measuring agent inter-prediction overlap. We measure predicted agent overlap on the best set of
L1012@P21: trajectory produced by the model. For the joint model, this corresponds to the joint prediction that
L1013@P21: has the higher probability score. For the marginal model, we take the top scoring trajectory for each
L1014@P21: agent to obtain the best set. For every predicted agent in the trajectory, we determine if it has an
L1015@P21: overlap with any other predicted agent by comparing the rotated upright 3D bounding boxes using
L1016@P21: our predicted xyz and heading. The inter-prediction overlap rate is the number of predicted agents
L1017@P21: that are involved in some overlap, divided by the total number of predicted agents. We count two
L1018@P21: agents as overlapping if the intersection over the union (IoU) exceeds 0.01.

L1030@P24: The Scene Transformer model is both agent permutation equivariant and scene-centric. These
L1031@P24: properties allow us to easily switch between a marginal vs joint loss formulation (Figure 8). In
L1032@P24: the marginal formulation, we reduce the loss of the best future for every agent separately; while in
L1033@P24: the joint formulation, we reduce the loss of the best future for all agents jointly. In practice, this
L1034@P24: determines when the reduce_min operation is performed.
